title: At home — and the passive you keep seeing
title_target: Rumah, kamar, dan kata kerja di-
goal: Describe where you live and what happens there, and finally understand the *di-* verbs that have been appearing on signs and menus since Unit 2 — Indonesian uses the passive far more than English does.
bekal: describe your house or room and what is in it
use *-nya* comfortably, in all three of its jobs

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Cari kos
dialogs.intro: Sarah is looking at a room in a boarding house. Bu Tuti is the owner.

lines.speaker: Tuti:
lines.id: Come in. This is the room.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.id: It's bright. Is there air conditioning?

lines.speaker: Tuti:
lines.text: Ada. Kamar mandi di dalam, air panas juga.
lines.id: Yes. Bathroom inside, and hot water too.
lines.literal: exist. room bathe at inside, water hot also.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Bagus. Kasur dan lemari sudah termasuk?
lines.id: Good. Are the bed and wardrobe included?
lines.literal: good. mattress and wardrobe already included?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.id: How much is the rent per month?

lines.speaker: Tuti:
lines.text: Dua juta lima ratus, sudah termasuk listrik.
lines.id: Two and a half million, electricity included.
lines.literal: two million five hundred, already included electricity.

lines.speaker: Tuti:
lines.text: Air gratis. Wifi juga, tapi kadang lambat.
lines.id: Water's free. Wifi too, but it's sometimes slow.
lines.literal: water free. wifi also, but sometimes slow.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.id: May I cook in the room?

lines.speaker: Tuti:
lines.text: Tidak boleh, tapi dapur bersama ada di bawah.
lines.id: No, but there's a shared kitchen downstairs.
lines.literal: not may, but kitchen together exist at below.

lines.speaker: Tuti:
lines.text: Boleh, sampai jam sembilan malam saja.
lines.id: Yes, until nine in the evening only.
lines.literal: may, until hour nine night only.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.id: All right, I'll take the room.

notes: **Semua sudah disediakan — "everything has been provided".** *Sedia* is "ready, available"; *menyediakan* is "to provide"; *disediakan* is "is provided". Indonesian reaches for the passive here where English might say "we provide everything", and that preference runs through the whole language.

**Kos** is a boarding house — a room in someone's property, rented monthly, and how most young Indonesians and many foreigners live. A *kos* with meals is *kos plus makan*; *kos putri* is for women only, *kos putra* for men.

**Sewanya berapa?** — the *-nya* again, meaning "its rent, the rent of this place". You have now met this suffix in *harganya*, *namanya*, *kamarnya*, *sewanya*. It is doing exactly the same job every time.
**AC is pronounced a-sé**, from the Dutch and English abbreviation, and it is the word everyone uses. *Kipas angin* is a fan — literally "wind fan".

**Prices for rooms are monthly and negotiable in a way shop prices are not.** *Kalau setahun, boleh kurang?* — "if I take it for a year, can you reduce it?" — is a completely normal question, and often works.

grammars.title: Di- : the passive you have been reading all along
body: Put *di-* in front of a root and the action happens **to** the subject. You have already been reading these for eighteen units.
after: The doer, when it is mentioned, follows with *oleh* ("by"): *Buku itu dibaca oleh Rina* — "that book is read by Rina". Most of the time it is simply left out, which is exactly why the passive is so convenient.

⚠️ Do not confuse the prefix *di-* with the preposition *di* ("at"). Written Indonesian keeps them apart: the preposition has a space (*di rumah*, at home), the prefix does not (*dijual*, is sold). It is one of the commonest spelling mistakes Indonesians themselves make.

grammars.title: The passive with a person doing it
body: When the doer is *saya*, *kamu* or *dia*, Indonesian uses a different, very common shape: pronoun straight before the bare verb, and no *di-* at all. You met it in Unit 13.
after: This is not a rare literary form; it is everyday Indonesian, and it is often preferred to the active *Saya sudah mengirimnya*. If you can say *Sudah saya kirim* naturally, you will sound noticeably more Indonesian than a learner who only ever builds active sentences.
Notice what it does to word order: the **thing** comes first, then the person, then the verb. Once you can hear that shape, a great many sentences that used to sound scrambled will suddenly resolve.

blocks.text: Housework verbs you will hear daily: *masak* (cook), *cuci* (wash), *sapu* (sweep), *bersihkan* (clean), *setrika* (iron), *buang sampah* (take the rubbish out), *jemur* (hang out to dry).
⚠️ A cultural note that saves confusion: shoes come off at the door of most Indonesian homes, and in many *kos*. If you see a row of sandals outside a door, add yours to it.
You have now met *-nya* a dozen times. Here is the whole picture in one place, because it is the single most frequent suffix in the language.

blocks.text: The first two lines are the same three words meaning two different things, and Indonesians never notice the ambiguity because the situation always resolves it. If you must be explicit, use *kamar dia* for "his room" and *kamar itu* for "that room".

Phrases with *-nya* that are worth knowing whole: *rasanya* (it feels/tastes), *kelihatannya* (it looks like), *sebaiknya* (it would be best to), *seharusnya* (it ought to be), *pokoknya* (the main thing is), *akhirnya* (finally).
